#2670. Cavaliers 115, Knicks 107: “Credit them, but…”

As sports fans, our teams give us plenty to think about and then some. They give us stuff to bicker, to complain, to ramble about. We follow their every move meticulously, we break down the potential of prospective grocery baggers and hail them as the next coming. We love to read or listen to others doing the same, even or especially if we do not agree with their viewpoints. Lucky fanatics get something to cheer about every once in a while – consider that box checked by our beloved New York Knickerbockers lately.

Understandably, that focus on one team, that love for one franchise can lead to kind of a narrow view on things at times. Nothing wrong with that; fandom doesn't have to be rational, it doesn't have to explain itself. And it does not necessarily have to involve the other team's perspective or, frankly, the other team at all. At times though, that group in the different colored jerseys is the biggest answer to the question you have regarding your own squad's performance.

Last night felt exactly like that kind of game where the Knicks did a lot of stuff well, but in the end the Cleveland Cavaliers just did most of it a little bit better. And when the Knicks didn't do something as well, it was also the Cavaliers who had a hand in that. From the opening tip, it was obvious that the Cavs wanted this one – analytically and this time around actually in reality, too. They remembered last Saturday when New York rained on their Rocket Arena parade on the second night of a back-to-back; they surely remembered the last time they visited Madison Square Garden. And it looked like they were tired of the narrative that had them as the soft wannabes that can't keep up when the orange and blue drivers push the pedals to the metal.

Donovan Mitchell lived in the lane for most of the night; every high slip screen was an automatic downhill and kick opportunity for the team from Ohio, and their old and new length bothered the smaller Knicks for long stretches of the game. Peyton Watson might not be able to hit the water from the Verrazzano Bridge right now, but he sure can impact a game defensively. A lot of the Ohioans were feeling good about themselves; Tyrese Proctor and Meleek Thomas gave youthful, quality energy off the bench. And then, of course, there was James Harden. That guy who is a poster child for a lot of ugly wrongs in the modern game, the one who has been awful all year long so far but decided to show up for this one and give his team a vintage performance in the very building he crapped the postseason bed in just half a year ago.

So even if, at least in Harden's case, it's hard to stomach, let's follow Knicks Fan in Jerusalem's proposal from the Postgame Thread that gave this text its headline. Let's credit the Cavaliers for a game well played, for shots hit, for storms weathered. But as the headline and our friend in Israel suggested, there's another side to the story, a "but". Tipping our collective cap to the Cavs sure doesn't mean the Knicks can't do a lot of things better in the future. Jalen Brunson had a good scoring game yet failed to deliver any rhythm to the offense. Too many times the ball just stuck on the perimeter (a particular problem for OG Anunoby right now), and there wasn't nearly enough off-ball movement to stretch a much bigger defense that wants you to finish over their size.

That size played quite a role in yesterday's contest, be it on the boards or in the passing lanes. Unfortunately, the Knicks won't get any taller, that's for sure. Mike Brown tried to counter Cleveland's length by going to Mohamed Diawara early in the absence of Jordan Clarkson. Mo had a nice drive and, in theory, could be a solution for physical matchup problems like this one, but clearly isn't there yet. The young Frenchman seems unsure about himself, plays hesitantly, and is missing the wide-open shots he knocked down in his sleep last season. His defense mostly looks good but not good enough to warrant a bigger role yet.

Aside from plenty of mental lapses, missing open shots was a problem for Josh Hart last night as well, but we excuse the veteran as he clearly had to shake off some rust after his injury break. That doesn't change the fact that his lack of consistent outside shooting can become an issue at times, especially against good teams that willingly put roaming defenders on him. Normally, he adds so many other intangibles that you can live with it in the bigger picture more often than not. In Mikal Bridges' case, though, well, what's there right now? Hounding defense? Don't see it consistently. A presence off the ball? Nope. Secondary scoring? Corner threes? Emotion? Desperation? Anything?

Bridges once again played an uneventful, meager 17 minutes in this one. Plenty of the other guards – Deuce McBride, Landry Shamet, and Tyler Kolek – currently do everything Bridges is paid for and actually a bit more. The longer this situation drags on, the louder Mike Brown will hear the question: When will you make a change to the starting lineup? It's easy to understand why he's reluctant; he sure doesn't want to create an internal problem by benching someone who did his part in winning a championship last year. But what if the problem is creating itself? There's a tipping point to everything.

For the Knicks, this game won't be one, and it shouldn't be. There might be some stuff to think about, though, going forward. Just like we want to have it as fans.

#2666. Dan Hicks, legendary NBC Sports and golf announcer, dies at age 64

Legendary NBC Sports broadcaster Dan Hicks died Wednesday following an acute illness, his family said in a statement. He was 64.

"Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan following an acute illness," Hicks' wife, Hannah Storm, said in a statement. "He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable.

"Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered.

"Our three daughters and I are heartbroken. We are grateful for the love and support surrounding our family during this incredibly difficult time. These are simply no words to express how much he will be missed."

Hicks was considered one of the preeminent sportscasters of his generation, calling a variety of high-profile events including the Olympics, PGA Tour and Notre Dame football.

After beginning his career at CNN, Hicks had been at NBC since 1992. He was a tower announcer for the network's golf coverage until being promoted to the lead play-by-play role in 2000. Among his most famous moments on the air, Hicks called Tiger Woods' dramatic putt to force a playoff at the 2008 U.S. Open as well as the U.S. swim team's stunning comeback at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. His partners in the booth included Johnny Miller and Rowdy Gaines.

#2662. 3 things to watch in 49ers-Cowboys: Run the football, Kyle

The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys will meet on Sunday and continue a storied history between the two franchises. What was once a rivalry has turned into an avalanche, with the 49ers' winning streak over the Cowboys spanning several years. Sunday is expected to be a high-scoring affair with two high-powered offenses, and Vegas believes it too, with the highest implied total of the weekend.

Former pass game coordinator and defensive backs coach for the Philadelphia Eagles under Vic Fangio, Christian Parker took over as defensive coordinator for Dallas this season, and let's just say things have not gone well. Kyle Shanahan and the 49ers know starting linebacker Dee Winters very well also. You can bet Shanahan and Brock Purdy will have the Cowboys' linebackers in a bind constantly on Sunday.

What else will the 49ers look to exploit on Sunday? Here are three things to watch for Sunday.

It may not feel like it, but the 49ers' rushing attack is number one in several reliable metrics. Not only are the 49ers number one in EPA/play (0.14), success rate (52.1%), and total EPA (66.26; Buffalo is second at 53.09), but they also lead in EPA/ rush, with Buffalo at 0.05 and a league-high success rate on the ground of 50.4%.

Dallas' defense ranks 27th in the NFL with an EPA/rush allowed of -0.02 and 25th in success rate allowed on the ground at 43.2%. After facing the worst run defense in the league in total rushing yards allowed last week, the 49ers face the second-worst run defense in Dallas with 1,327 rushing yards allowed and 4.99 rushing yards per attempt.

Even pushing to a heavier box count is unlikely, as Dallas has an 18.1% rate. That number is good for 30th in the NFL. That 40-carry number is in the 49ers' sights for a second consecutive week.

The 49ers hold a slight edge in motion percentage over the Miami Dolphins at 73.% to Miami's 73.2% for the league high mark. It's not just the amount of motion, but the types of motions, which include the often-used banana motions from Kyle Juszczyk. The advantages of the motion in the run game, to change number counts, and in the pass game to help identify coverages are a huge part of the offense.

Dallas is dead last with a 0.11 EPA allowed per play against motion. Good luck, Dallas. The 49ers rank fourth in motion at snap with 50.6%.

Dak Prescott against the 49ers' preferred coverages

DAZN Bet Alberta offers many ways to wager on your favorite sports. These include the most common methods like moneyline, point spread, totals, parlays, props, and futures, but there are also system bets (round robin) and teasers.

Moneyline: Pick a winner. Those with "-" odds are the favorite; "+" odds are the underdog.

Point spread: This is a number designed to make a game as close as possible. If a team is -3.5, they need to win outright by 4 points or more; if a team is +3.5, they can cover by winning the game or losing by 3 points or fewer. The odds are almost always -110.

Totals: The odds on these markets are also almost always -110, and you'll wager on whether a point total will fall short or exceed a number.

Parlays: Combine multiple events together. For a parlay to succeed, all legs must win.

Futures: Wager on events that'll resolve later, such as the Super Bowl winner.

Props: Wager on player performance, such as quarterback passing yards, hits in a baseball game, or rebounds in basketball.

Same Game Parlays: Same as a standard parlay, only instead it's focused on one game.

System:  Another term for Round Robin, this will allow you to wager on multiple iterations of a parlay, such as a 4-leg parlay having 6 2-leg parlay options.

Teasers: Altering the point spread or totals in your favor while sacrificing some odds value. For example, if you had a 2-leg parlay with two NFL teams with a point spread of -7 and you did a 6-point teaser, their new spread is now just -1.

#2659. Should the Titans re-sign Tony Pollard after declining to trade him?

The Tennessee Titans were very active leading up to the NFL trade deadline. They traded Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, and Amani Hooker to the Buffalo Bills. By doing so, Mike Borgonzi acquired four total picks, including two first-rounders for Simmons, and an additional second-rounder for Hooker.

One player who was not traded was running back Tony Pollard. Reports had consistently indicated the Titans preferred to hold onto Pollard because he's been helping with the development and evaluation of Cam Ward. Regardless of how that makes you feel, it seems those reports were accurate.

Pollard is in a contract year. It was previous GM Ran Carthon who signed the former Memphis standout to a three-year, $21.7 million contract prior to the 2024 campaign. Pollard is currently the 22nd-highest paid back in the league, proving that contract has aged well.

But declining opportunities to trade a 29-year-old RB on an expiring contract when you're rebuilding the roster is an interesting tactic. It makes us wonder if Borgonzi is considering re-signing Pollard. He's due for unrestricted free agency.

The running back market has been reset by recent deals for Bijan Robinson, Jahmyr Gibbs, and Saquon Barkley. They are among four RBs earning more than $20 million annually (alongside Jonathan Taylor). Pollard obviously isn't that tier of back, but the increases in pay will impact his negotiations, too.

Given Pollard's age, the Titans shouldn't re-sign him to longer than a two-year extension. Given his advancing age, they'll want to protect themselves against overpaying for a declining talent. Signing Pollard to a two-year, $20 million contract feels fair.

Pollard would earn $10 million annually, making him the 16th-highest paid back in the NFL right behind Kyren Williams ($11m AAV). Other happenings around the league might impact this, but that feels like the appropriate range for a Pollard extension.

#2658. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2656. "We hope he makes the right choice" – Mancini on Tresoldi's decision between Germany and Italy

Eligible to represent both countries, Nicolo Tresoldi remains undecided over whether to play for Germany or Italy at senior international level.

The 22-year-old German U21 international has so far made himself unavailable for selection by either senior national team as he carefully considers which country to represent.

As Italy head coach Roberto Mancini revealed at a press conference on Monday, he and technical director Claudio Ranieri have both held talks with Tresoldi, hoping the Club Brugge forward will ultimately choose the Azzurri.

"I spoke to Tresoldi, and Ranieri did too. But I believe he must feel that he wants to play for the national team," Mancini said, via Football Italia.

"His father is Italian; he won the Euros with the U21s. I think there's a chance. He knows he can be an important player for the future; we hope he makes the right choice."

Tresoldi is currently with the German U21 national team, preparing for their upcoming games against Belgium and Croatia.

#2654. John Harbaugh: tonight’s Commanders-Giants game “is for all the marbles” - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

The thing about firing Dan Quinn as coach of the Washington Commanders — though it would placate an increasingly dissatisfied fanbase — is there's a trickledown that would leave the franchise in a state that has defined it for far too long: unstable.

Bear with me, because a vote for the status quo could seem — how to put this? — wild at the moment. This isn't a case that Quinn should keep his job based on his team's current trajectory as much as it is a warning about what would follow if the losses continue.

When things are going as they are — and Washington is 4-15-1 over the last 13 months — people tend to want heads to roll. Change becomes the only way to satisfy that. It's an emotional response, which is fine, because what's the point in rooting for a sports franchise if it doesn't manage to tap into your emotions?

But think about the fallout if Quinn and his staff don't survive. Their fate hangs in the remaining results, which must start improving beginning Thursday night against the New York Giants at the Meadowlands. There are a host of reasons any Commanders fan who is interested in the long-term stability and success of the franchise should root for a turnaround.

[Josh Harris's] record in the other two American sports franchises he owns would suggest Harris isn't afraid of change. That's good. A willingness to admit mistakes should be a trait of a good owner.

But if Quinn is ousted after his third season, wouldn't the start to Harris' stewardship feel — and it's scary to go here — a little Snyder-esque?

The way to avoid that: Have Quinn and his crew turn this season around. At this point, that might seem unlikely, but in the interest of distancing this franchise from the previous quarter-century, it would be the best outcome for everyone — from the quarterback to the fans.

Daniels came into 2026 ready to reset after missing 10 games due to injury last season. The Commanders were also in reset mode. They kept head coach Dan Quinn in place, but swapped out both coordinators. On Daniels's side of the ball, they promoted David Blough to become their new OC and implement a more traditional, under-center style of offense—a significant change after primarily running a no-huddle, shotgun offense under Kliff Kingsbury. They also made numerous roster changes, primarily on the defensive side of the ball as they looked to improve one of the worst-ranked defenses in the NFL during the 2025 campaign.

The new offense has brought mixed results. There are times that Daniels and the offense are in rhythm, such as in the first half of their game against the Rams, when they got out to a 10–6 halftime lead. At other times, they struggle to move the ball at all, such as in the second half or their loss to the Rams, when they couldn't muster a single first down in the third quarter.

The Commanders' offense ranks 20th in yards per game (325.4) and passing yards per game (207.4), 21st in points per game (21) and 22nd in EPA per play (-0.08). They are undermanned due to injuries to their best offensive lineman, Laremy Tunsil, and receiver, Terry McLaurin, but also aren't fully playing up to their potential.

Aside from some game management miscues, Daniels is still playing well, even if he's not quite lifting the team the way he did as a rookie.

While McCarthy has changed teams and other quarterbacks from the class saw their teams undergo coaching changes early on (Michael Penix Jr., Caleb Williams and Drake Maye), Daniels could be facing that fate in Year 4 if the Commanders move on from Quinn.

The Commanders have their quarterback in Daniels, but with low playoff hopes (a win Thursday would draw them to two games behind the Giants in the NFC East, while the wild-card field is crowded) and a franchise still figuring out how to properly build around him, his career is at an odd standstill. He is not trending downward, but he has also not built off that wondrous rookie campaign.

The Giants are third in the NFL in passing defense, giving up only 177.8 yards per game, and fifth in total defense. They haven't been as strong, though, at stopping the run. New York is 21st in yards allowed per game, with 123.6 yards per game and 4.7 yards per carry. Washington is 11th in rushing offense and eighth in yards per carry despite injuries in the backfield. Jacory Croskey-Merritt was lost to an injured groin, while Jemery McNichols faces potential foot surgery two games after briefly returning from IR. Right now, the Commanders' running backs are Rachaad White, Austin Ekeler, and Robert Henry. And there's always the running threat of quarterback Jayden Daniels. Rachaad White showed flashes a week ago, but Washington needs to establish their ground game early and often to keep New York on its toes.

QB stat to know: Jayden Daniels has thrown seven touchdowns and no interceptions. This team has little margin for error, and turnovers would bury it. Second-half storyline: Dan Quinn's job security. Washington's first-half schedule was difficult but it should be better than 2-5-1. Here is one thing we know about the Giants' plans to beat the Commanders: they are going to put pressure on Daniels.

The Giants' defense has continued to improve from the last time the two teams squared off in Week 5. They are now fifth in yards allowed and third against the pass, allowing just 178 yards through the air. Part of that is a credit to how much pressure they put on opposing quarterbacks; they rank third in blitz percentage, according to Pro Football Reference, and considering that they pressured Daniels on nearly 30% of his dropbacks in Week 5, you can expect something similar in Week 10.

Here's the silver lining for the Commanders, though: while the Giants do blitz more than almost any team, it has not led to pressures. They rank last in pressure rate (18.9%) and only have 16 sacks for the season. In fact, rookie Arvell Reese is the only Giants defender with more than two sacks on the year.

Although it might not feel like it after allowing four sacks against the Los Angeles Rams, the Commanders are around league average in sacks allowed and rank sixth in pass block win rate, per ESPN. That isn't going to stop the Giants from trying, though, so it will be important for Washington's offensive line to give Daniels time to work. If the blitzes keep coming, there will be areas for him to exploit downfield.

I really want to believe in the Commanders. I picked them to upset the Los Angeles Rams last week, and it was an extremely even game. The Rams going 3-for-3 on fourth down and Myles Garrett being active decided the game. You could make a case that Dan Quinn's team got unlucky, but I won't do that. When something happens repeatedly, it's not luck. Unfortunately, losing close games seems woven into the fabric of the 2026 Commanders, perhaps as karmic payback for a 2024 iteration that seemingly won every close game and converted every fourth down en route to a surprise appearance in the NFC Championship Game.

The Giants are 4-1-1 in one-score games. That tie came against these Commanders in a game that Washington absolutely should have won — and I'm a Giants fan saying that. John Harbaugh is just a better coach than Quinn. It is what it is.

Obviously, the Commanders have the better quarterback. Daniels is still electric, and J.J. McCarthy was not good in the win at Philly. I just have faith that the Giants will make plays when they need to, and the Commanders not only won't but will actively hurt their own chances at winning.

What else is there to say about this offense? I keep sitting down to write these reviews hoping that the film will give me something different to discuss. Instead, the Eagles ended up with 220 yards of offense, 13 first downs, and an average of 3.3 yards per play. They had the ball for nine and a half fewer minutes than the Giants. Another week, another miserable offensive performance. Hooray!

Joe Milton gave us a few things to enjoy. His mobility prevented an already awful performance from looking even worse, and there were a couple of throws that showed why his arm talent is intriguing. But changing the quarterback hasn't changed how I feel watching this offense. It is still boring, disjointed, and far too difficult. At this point, I want this staff to move on so I can start looking forward to a new season. It's November! I'd like to feel excited about the Eagles' offense again.

Although it seemed at times that they would find a way to lose the game, the Dallas Cowboys managed to prevail over the Indianapolis Colts. It didn't exactly save a season that still is teetering on the edge of the precipice, and any good feelings from this win are likely to dissipate when Dallas host the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. Our Tom Ryle and Sean Martin take a look at what faces the Cowboys.

I have to compare the narrow 27-23 win over the Colts to cotton candy. We wanted it, but it turned out to be messy and rather unsatisfying.

And it didn't exactly presage a strong showing against the Niners, who are one of the best teams in the league. While Dallas has managed to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory more than once this season, San Francisco keeps finding ways to win with an injury list that runs on and on. They have a clearly winning culture, while the Cowboys have something. And there is absolutely no comparison between the head coaches.

If Dallas loses, especially by double digits, I think there will just be a sense of resignation and no expectations that the Cowboys can claw their way back into the playoffs.

The worst thing is how this all seems largely irrelevant. Not only have the Cowboys done nothing to really make us think they can win, they have also shown no carryover from a previous win.

And if they do lose, we can just relax and start digging into potential draft picks and replacements for the coaching staff.

Week 10 will be telling when it comes to the Giants' path to an NFC East title

[T]his week could provide a massive swing for the Giants.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh was speaking specifically about the Commanders when he said the following, but the idea he was getting at applies to the week and the division as a whole:

"This is for all the marbles. It's a tie right now. This is the tiebreaker. It's like going to the second half tied, you have a chance to go win the game right now and be one up on these guys for the rest of the season. So, it's a big game."

If the Giants lose Thursday and Dallas upsets the 49ers, this is what the NFC East would look like:

Dallas would be just 1.5 games back, and the Commanders would be back in the hunt with eight games remaining.

Teams have combined to score 45.93 points per game this season, according to NFL Research. That's down slightly from 46.74 points per game halfway through last season, and a tick higher than the 45.36 points per game after nine weeks in 2024.

The league has seen plenty of close finishes this season. Through nine weeks, 77 games have come down to one score (eight or fewer points). That ties the 2016 season for the third-most through Week 9 in NFL history, trailing only the 2024 (79) and 2022 (79) seasons.

Of those 77 games, 41 have featured a game-winning score in the final five minutes of regulation or overtime. That's the second-most through Week 9, trailing only the 2021 season, which featured 42 such finishes. In 25 games, the winning team rallied from at least 10 points down, which ties the 2011 season for the fourth-most in league history. That figure trails the 1987 (30), 2020 (26) and 2022 (26) seasons.

The changes have seemingly done the trick, as the number of kickoff returns (1,118) and kickoff return yards (28,896) mark the most in league history through nine weeks.

If the Penguins continue to occupy the bottom of the Eastern Conference, Dubas will face tough decisions. He has a handful of stars on expiring or soon-to-be-expiring contracts, and those players could be very attractive to other teams. Erik Karlsson seems like and obvious trade candidate. But if there was a fire sale, would Dubas go as far as shipping out a franchise icon?

Look, it's still very early, and there are reasons to believe a turnaround is coming. The Penguins' five-on-five numbers are far better than the results indicate, and Crosby is fully capable of shaking off a slow start and hitting another level.

#2649. Bengals sent Zac Taylor to clear the Eagles’ name in failed Arnold Ebiketie trade

The Eagles and Bengals thought they had a deal in place to send Arnold Ebiketie from Philadelphia to Cincinnati, but just an hour after the trade was announced, it had reportedly been canceled. Insiders like Adam Schefter were quick to report that the trade falling apart was not due to a physical or performance concern, and it was eventually revealed to be a miscalculation on what Ebiketie would cost the team.

Initial trade terms was sending a sixth-round draft pick to the Eagles in exchange for the OLB, but since Ebiketie was a compensatory free agent, trading for him would negate the Bengals future third-round comp pick from the Trey Hendrickson trade. Adding in the loss of a third-rounder, in addition to the agreed upon sixth-round pick, made the trade to expensive for Cincinnati, so they bailed on the deal.

Instead of speaking to reporters about the incident himself, Bengals GM Duke Tobin sent a message via head coach Zac Taylor about the situation — who admitted he didn't really feel comfortable with the specific way Tobin wanted things portrayed —, but wanted it to be clear that Howie Roseman and the Eagles were good trade partners.

Mike Garafolo said that the vibes inside the Eagles building were very angry, and how teams move in these situations can absolutely affect future trades and team's willingness to do business together. Taylor shouldn't have been the messenger, but it was important for Tobin to clear the air and make sure this move wouldn't even further affect the Eagles in a negative way.

#2642. MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League proposes delaying salary cap for 'smoother transition'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

The collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

To allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system."

MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

In its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:

How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:

All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:

Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits."

The timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

Commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for."

"The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer says of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance issues in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse."

The MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:

The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

More face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:

MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full:

"The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

"Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a new 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

"We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans."

"After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

"The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

"Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing new, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations."

Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:

"Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans."

As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:

Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:

Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

"It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."

Speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

"We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us."

In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

"Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."

Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion."

"Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table."

MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:

Using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:

"Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide."

"We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin says in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll."

Negotiations on a new CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

#2640. MLB proposes delaying salary cap in new negotiations as Dec. 1 CBA expiration inches nearer

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the implementation of a salary cap/floor system until 2028 as part of its latest collective bargaining agreement proposal, the league announced Tuesday. MLB says the delay is intended to provide a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system and give teams more time to prepare and get their payrolls in order.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool, and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."

The league also newly proposed a $180.2 million salary floor and a $258.2 million salary cap. Those numbers are up from $171.2 million and $245.3 million, respectively, in the league's previous proposal in June. The $1 million minimum salary would only apply to players with at least two years of service time. The minimum salary would be $900,000 for all other players.

Four teams currently have more than $258.2 million on the books for 2027 (including arbitration projections) and 20 teams have less than $180.2 million on the books, according to FanGraphs' calculations. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027 before the transition to a salary cap/floor system in 2028.

The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time. The previous lockout ended on March 10, then there was a three-week spring training leading up to Opening Day. If there is a similarly lengthy lockout, it would be impossible for clubs to become salary cap-compliant in such a short period of time.

The MLB Players Association has repeatedly insisted it will not accept a salary cap/floor system, and has instead proposed a revised revenue sharing system that would funnel more money from big-market teams to small-market teams. In a statement following the league's proposal on Tuesday, the MLBPA accused owners of continuing to "propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The union also said that even with a delayed implementation, the league's proposal of a salary cap maintains the same "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights, including guaranteed contracts."

MLB says its push for a salary cap/floor system is intended to improve competitive balance. The small-market Milwaukee Brewers defeated the small-market Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series last week and swept big-market teams (Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees) en route to the Fall Classic.

#2638. MLB offseason bold predictions: Tarik Skubal breaks records, World Series champ gets a deal, a FA frenzy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the Brewers crowned World Series champions, the 2026-27 offseason is underway. We're still waiting for the first significant free agent signing or trade, which isn't unusual less than a week into the offseason. Give it another week or so and the action will pick up. Before the hot stove really gets burning, here are 10 bold predictions for the 2026-27 offseason. Remember, all geniuses were called crazy at first.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract in history, and our first bold prediction says Tarik Skubal, this offseason's undisputed No. 1 free agent, will beat that. Specifically, he'll sign a contract that is closer to $400 million in value than $300 million, which is another way of saying he'll clear $350 million and break Yamamoto's record for total dollars by a good bit. Scott Boras, Skubal's agent, likes to break contract records with room to spare, not just by a tiny bit. Skubal is the best free agent starter since Yamamoto, and the best free agent starter with MLB experience since Gerrit Cole in 2019. It's a very thin free agent class with few places to (wisely) spend money. The bet here is a team steps up and gives Skubal a record deal.

Milwaukee's thing over the last few years has been trading its top players a year before free agency (Corbin Burnes, Freddy Peralta, Devin Williams, etc.) and obviously it has worked for them. William Contreras is at that point now: he's scheduled to hit the open market next offseason. This next bold prediction says the Brewers will buck that trend and instead sign the World Series MVP to a long-term extension that keeps him in Milwaukee for at least another few years, if not the rest of his career. How does six years at $24 million a pop sound? That would be $144 million total and the richest contract given to a catcher in the last 13 years, clearing Will Smith's $140 extension with the Dodgers. The World Series champs keep their most irreplaceable player. It has been foretold.

Every offseason is important, and this one is extra important for new Astros GM Randy Flores, who must figure out what to do with third baseman Isaac Paredes and shortstop Jeremy Peña, both a year away from free agency. Keeping Peña and trading Paredes, and installing Carlos Correa at the hot corner, is the sensible move. This bold prediction says the opposite will happen. The Astros will trade Peña and keep Paredes, and figure out their 2027 infield alignment later. Houston needs help up and down the roster, particularly on the mound, and I think the offers for Peña will simply be too great for Flores to ignore. It will be similar to the Kyle Tucker trade two years ago. The Astros don't have to move Peña, but the offers will get to a point where they just can't say no.

On one hand, keeping the offense intact and adding some pitching would be a viable offseason plan for the Braves. On the other hand, can they really run it back with the same offense that flatlined after June 1 and in the NLDS? It might be time to shake things up a bit, and I boldly predict it will happen. Ronald Acuña Jr., Drake Baldwin, Michael Harris II, and Matt Olson aren't going anywhere. No team will take the current version of Austin Riley and the six years (!) remaining on his contract. That leaves Ozzie Albies and I suppose Sean Murphy, though the latter is well into role player status now. Does that make this bold prediction a "the Braves will trade Albies" prediction? Yeah, I guess it does. It feels like things are getting a little stale in Atlanta and it's time to change up a core.

You could argue Freddy Peralta is the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal. You could also argue it's Trevor Rogers, who doesn't have Peralta's pedigree or track record, but has strong under-the-hood performance indicators, the kind that project well into the future and get players paid. So, for this bold prediction, I'll say that Rogers signs a richer deal than Peralta, even though the latter is the more famous player and has been better in their careers to date. It'll be close. I can see Rogers getting something in the $125 million range and Peralta signing for right around $120 million, but, in the end, Rogers will sign for more guaranteed dollars because he's a year and a half younger and teams love nothing more than players they believe have untapped upside. That's Rogers, not Peralta.

After the Dodgers swept in the NLCS, there were calls to infuse some youth into the roster, and, honestly, they need it. Fortunately, Los Angeles has one of the best prospects in the game in the precocious Josue De Paula, who was so impressive late in the season. Trading an outfielder to clear a spot for De Paula seems like such an obvious move that I'm not sure this prediction qualifies as bold. Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere, which leaves Teoscar Hernández. How about a trade that sends Hernández back to the Blue Jays? It's a one-year commitment, the Blue Jays badly need over-the-fence power, and the fan base already loves the guy. Teoscar to Toronto as what amounts to their George Springer replacement. I boldly predict it.

Every offseason, there are two teams that appear to match up so well that a trade feels inevitable. Last offseason, it was the Brewers and Mets for a Freddy Peralta deal. This offseason, it's the Cubs and Yankees. The Cubs need rotation help and have some young position players to spare (like Matt Shaw). The Yankees need infield help and have starting pitching to trade (like Will Warren). I'm not saying Shaw for Warren will happen or even should happen. I'm just saying Chicago's and New York's trade chips and roster needs align very well, and when that happens, a trade typically comes together. This bold prediction says the Cubs will send a position player to the Yankees for a starting pitcher, with maybe some other pieces involved on both sides.

There are trade rumors involving a Mariners starting pitcher every offseason and there's a good reason for that. They have a lot of really good starters and teams want them. The Mariners currently have Kade Anderson, Logan Gilbert, Emerson Hancock, George Kirby, Bryce Miller, and Bryan Woo lined up for their 2027 rotation. They could keep them all because pitching depth has a way of disappearing, sure, but Seattle needed another bat even before Randy Arozarena became a free agent. This next bold prediction says the Mariners finally trade one of their starters in an arm-for-bat deal. I'll say Kirby, who is two years away from free agency, is the one to go. Gilbert is a one-year rental but the better pitcher. The others all have longer control than Kirby.

After coming out of the gate so well in April and May, Munetaka Murakami finished right where the pundits expected. He hit .207 and had the highest strikeout rate among qualified hitters, but he also slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games. Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato, who will be posted for MLB teams this offseason, is similar to Murakami as a strikeout-prone lefty with huge power. This bold prediction says Sato will double Murakami's contract with the White Sox (two years and $34 million) because he's a better bet to stay at third base, a position that is barren in free agency, and because Murakami provided proof of concept. He showed that a player with big contact concerns in Japan can indeed succeed stateside, even if it is an eyesore at times. Four years and $68 million for Sato, perhaps with an opt out that makes the $68 million not really $68 million.

Dec. 1 is of course when the collective bargaining agreement expires and the owners are expected to lock out the players. My final bold prediction says free agents and teams will get out ahead of the potential lockout and sign in November. Players won't want to wait until who knows when to sign and teams will want to lock in contracts so they can be grandfathered into whatever the next CBA brings. MLB free agency tends to be slow-moving. Last offseason, only one of our top 10 free agents signed in November, and that was Shota Imanaga taking the qualifying offer. Only three other top 10 free agents signed in December. The other six signed on Jan. 14 or later. This offseason will be the opposite, I boldly predict. There will be a flurry of activity in November and at least seven of our top 10 free agents will put pen to paper before a potential lockout.
